name: why-we-say-hello
narration: You say it every single day. To strangers, to friends, to empty rooms. You've never once thought about where it came from. That story is about to change. Before 1877, almost nobody said hello as a greeting. The word existed, but it was a shout. You'd shout it to flag down a ferryman across water. It meant stop and listen, nothing more. That was not how you walked into a room. For centuries, greetings had a fixed shape. Good morning. Good afternoon. How do you do. They told you the time, the name, the register. A greeting carried real information, not just noise. Then the telephone arrived and changed all of that fast. The year is 1876, and Bell invented the telephone. Two people could now speak from different buildings, different cities. It was extraordinary and it created one problem. Nobody knew what to say when they picked it up. Think about how strange that actually was. The telephone was magic, but it had no manual. Nobody had designed a protocol for this moment. When you walked toward someone, you could see them. You knew the time of day. You knew exactly who was standing there. The telephone strips every single one of those cues away. You lift the receiver and someone is there. You have no idea who is on the line. There was no script for this moment. Bell had his answer. That answer was Ahoy. A nautical term Dutch sailors used to hail ships. Bell liked it, clear, loud, and already in use. He believed Ahoy was obviously the right word. But Thomas Edison had a completely different answer. Edison was building and running his own telephone exchanges. In August 1877, Edison wrote one letter. Hello, he said, can be heard twenty feet away. Clean, loud, no nautical baggage, no prior meaning. His reasoning was simple and completely practical. No sentiment. No poetry. Just what works over a wire. Edison ran the exchanges. He chose the word. Switchboard women across America became the hello girls. Not the ahoy girls. Not the good morning girls. Hello girls. The word was now inside every exchange. Bell kept saying Ahoy for the rest of his life. But he lost the word war. His own invention buried his preferred greeting. Think about how that must have felt for Bell. He invented the thing that killed his greeting. And then something unexpected happened: Hello escaped the telephone. It had started as a machine word, nothing more. Something you said only into a device. But within a decade, people said it face to face. The telephone had given the world a new word. And the word refused to stay on the wire. By the late 1880s, hello was appearing in books. By the 1890s, it was in songs and plays. By 1900, children used it without ever owning a telephone. The word had completely outrun its own origin story. No other word had ever traveled quite this way. Not through generations, not through religion, not through conquest. It spread through copper wire in under twenty years. Today, Germany says hallo. France says allô. Latin America says aló. Almost every language borrowed it. And almost all of them got it through the telephone. In every language, in every country, in every home. Because of one man, with one phone, with one letter. One letter written in 1877 became the planet's greeting. You say it every single day. To strangers, to friends, to empty rooms. Hello. That is Edison's word. It is still winning.

shots.phrase: You say it every single day.
shots.scene: Bo waves hello to passersby at a sunny sidewalk café table, morning light, warm cobblestone street background — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: To strangers, to friends, to empty rooms.
shots.scene: Bo turns to wave at three things in sequence — a stranger walking past, a friend at a nearby table, then an empty chair — expression playful — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: You've never once thought about where it came from.
shots.scene: Bo pauses mid-wave, tilts his head, squints at the air with a genuinely puzzled expression, one finger raised — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: That story is about to change.
shots.scene: Bo turns directly to the viewer, points at them with a knowing grin, eyebrows raised — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Before 1877, almost nobody said hello as a greeting.
shots.scene: Bo stands beside a large vintage calendar showing 1876, gestures at two supporting figures in Victorian frock coats exchanging formal bows instead of saying hello — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: The word existed, but it was a shout.
shots.scene: Bo cups both hands around his mouth, body leaning forward in a full shouting stance, expression strained with effort — full-body wide shot, open misty field background

shots.phrase: You'd shout it to flag down a ferryman across water.
shots.scene: Bo stands at a muddy riverbank shouting across the water while a supporting figure in period clothing rows a wooden skiff toward him — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: It meant stop and listen, nothing more.
shots.scene: Bo holds one palm flat out in a stop gesture while pointing at his ear with the other hand, expression firm and instructive — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: That was not how you walked into a room.
shots.scene: Bo steps through a doorway into a Victorian parlor where supporting figures in top hats and gowns trade elaborate 'good mornings' — Bo watches with eyebrows raised at the contrast — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: For centuries, greetings had a fixed shape.
shots.scene: Bo studies a tall illustrated timeline of historical greetings mounted on a library wall, tracing it slowly with his finger — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Good morning. Good afternoon. How do you do.
shots.scene: Bo watches two supporting figures in Victorian dress exchange exaggerated formal greetings — hat tips, hand kisses, bows — Bo looks amused and slightly bewildered — full-body wide shot, cobblestone street

shots.phrase: They told you the time, the name, the register.
shots.scene: Bo points at three things the supporting figures reveal in turn — a pocket watch, a printed name card, a social-rank badge — Bo nodding with interest — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: A greeting carried real information, not just noise.
shots.scene: Bo holds a formal calling card reading 'Good Morning, Sir' and examines it like an important document — expression thoughtful and impressed — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Then the telephone arrived and changed all of that fast.
shots.scene: Bo steps back in shock as a large wooden telephone contraption crashes down from the sky into the town square, startling two supporting figures — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: The year is 1876, and Bell invented the telephone.
shots.scene: Bo stands beside a large '1876' street sign while a supporting figure in a Victorian coat (playing Bell, with period side whiskers) holds a bulky wooden telephone proudly — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Two people could now speak from different buildings, different cities.
shots.scene: Bo holds one telephone receiver while pointing across to a distant building on the horizon where a supporting figure holds the other end — Bo's expression amazed — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: It was extraordinary and it created one problem.
shots.scene: Bo stares at the telephone with genuine wonder, then notices a giant floating question mark hanging above the receiver — expression shifting from awe to concern — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Nobody knew what to say when they picked it up.
shots.scene: Bo lifts a telephone receiver to his ear, mouth open and completely frozen, eyes darting — supporting figures around him equally paralyzed with the same problem — full-body wide shot, 1880s exchange room

shots.phrase: Think about how strange that actually was.
shots.scene: Bo sets the receiver down and turns to the viewer, gestures around with both hands — expression of genuine disbelief — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: The telephone was magic, but it had no manual.
shots.scene: Bo holds the telephone in one hand and a completely blank open book labeled 'USER MANUAL' in the other, looking back and forth between them — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Nobody had designed a protocol for this moment.
shots.scene: Bo points at a large blank rulebook on a desk and shrugs with both arms wide while supporting figures around him hold phones and stare at each other in confusion — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: When you walked toward someone, you could see them.
shots.scene: Bo walks down a sunny cobblestone street toward a supporting figure, their eyes meeting across the lane — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: You knew the time of day.
shots.scene: Bo glances up at a large clock tower, nods with certainty — full-body wide shot, town square background

shots.phrase: You knew exactly who was standing there.
shots.scene: Bo points confidently at the approaching supporting figure who wears a visible name plate on their lapel — Bo looks sure of himself — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: The telephone strips every single one of those cues away.
shots.scene: Bo gestures toward the clock, the name tag, and the face of the supporting figure — all three dissolve away one by one, leaving only a black telephone — Bo stares at it alone — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: You lift the receiver and someone is there.
shots.scene: Bo carefully lifts a black Bakelite telephone receiver with both hands, eyes wide and cautious, the exchange room humming quietly behind him — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: You have no idea who is on the line.
shots.scene: Bo holds the receiver to his ear with a completely baffled expression, a giant question mark hovering above his head — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: There was no script for this moment.
shots.scene: Bo frantically flips through an empty blank notebook, finding nothing on any page — expression increasingly desperate — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Bell had his answer. That answer was Ahoy.
shots.scene: Bo turns to see a supporting figure in a 1870s frock coat (playing Bell, with full period side whiskers) standing confidently and pointing to 'AHOY' written in a speech bubble — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: A nautical term Dutch sailors used to hail ships.
shots.scene: Bo looks surprised as two supporting figures in sailor outfits appear, waving their hats and shouting 'Ahoy!' at a painted ship on a harbor backdrop behind them — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Bell liked it, clear, loud, and already in use.
shots.scene: Bell figure (supporting) demonstrates bellowing 'Ahoy!' while Bo watches beside him, arms crossed, nodding slowly with a slightly skeptical expression — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: He believed Ahoy was obviously the right word.
shots.scene: Bell figure (supporting) plants an 'AHOY' flag in the ground and crosses his arms proudly — Bo raises one eyebrow at the viewer — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: But Thomas Edison had a completely different answer.
shots.scene: Bo turns as a supporting figure in a rumpled coat and wide-brimmed hat (playing Edison) strides in confidently from the opposite side of the frame, holding a notepad — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Edison was building and running his own telephone exchanges.
shots.scene: Edison figure (supporting) gestures proudly at rows of telephone switchboards behind him while Bo looks around the busy room, genuinely impressed — full-body wide shot, 1870s exchange interior

shots.phrase: In August 1877, Edison wrote one letter.
shots.scene: Edison figure (supporting) sits writing at a cluttered desk while Bo leans over his shoulder to read — Bo's eyes widen as he scans the page — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Hello, he said, can be heard twenty feet away.
shots.scene: Bo watches Edison figure shout 'HELLO' as a measuring tape unfurls in the air showing '20 FEET' and the word travels clearly across the entire room — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Clean, loud, no nautical baggage, no prior meaning.
shots.scene: Bo holds up a glowing 'HELLO' sign while pointing to a crossed-out ship anchor and a crossed-out nautical chart — expression approving — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: His reasoning was simple and completely practical.
shots.scene: Bo points at Edison's letter on the desk, expression shifting from curious to genuinely convinced — Bo gives a slow, acknowledging nod — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: No sentiment. No poetry. Just what works over a wire.
shots.scene: Bo mimes eliminating flourishes with both hands — sweeping away invisible decorations — then holds up a copper wire and gives it a decisive thumbs up — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Edison ran the exchanges. He chose the word.
shots.scene: Edison figure (supporting) stamps 'HELLO' in red ink on a large official document at the head of a switchboard room — Bo watches with arms folded — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Switchboard women across America became the hello girls.
shots.scene: Bo stands in a 1880s telephone exchange room as three supporting figures in period shirtwaists work the switchboards, each wearing a small badge reading 'Hello Girl' — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Not the ahoy girls. Not the good morning girls.
shots.scene: Bo turns to a chalk wall and crosses out 'AHOY GIRLS' and 'GOOD MORNING GIRLS' one by one, shaking his head each time — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Hello girls. The word was now inside every exchange.
shots.scene: Bo gestures at the full exchange room where every supporting figure speaks into a telephone using 'Hello!' speech bubbles — the room buzzing with the word — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Bell kept saying Ahoy for the rest of his life.
shots.scene: An older Bell supporting figure (grey hair, same side whiskers) stubbornly holds up an 'AHOY' placard while Bo stands nearby watching, one hand on chin — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: But he lost the word war.
shots.scene: Bo points at a scoreboard on the wall showing HELLO: 1,000,000 — AHOY: 1 — Bo looks at the viewer with an expressive 'it's over' face — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: His own invention buried his preferred greeting.
shots.scene: Bo watches as a large wooden telephone model falls onto a pile of 'AHOY' papers, flattening them completely — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Think about how that must have felt for Bell.
shots.scene: Bo turns directly to the viewer, places one hand over his chest with a genuinely sympathetic expression, eyebrows pulled up — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: He invented the thing that killed his greeting.
shots.scene: Bo mimes the irony — points at a telephone, then at a crossed-out 'AHOY', then slowly shakes his head — expression of wry, genuine tragedy — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: And then something unexpected happened: Hello escaped the telephone.
shots.scene: Bo watches in surprise as the glowing word 'HELLO' bursts out of a telephone receiver and flies across the room — Bo's eyes track it in disbelief — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: It had started as a machine word, nothing more.
shots.scene: Bo points at a telephone with 'HELLO' stenciled on its side like a machine label — just a device word — expression matter-of-fact — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Something you said only into a device.
shots.scene: Bo mimes picking up a telephone, says 'hello' into it, then sets it down and walks away — the word stays tethered to the device — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: But within a decade, people said it face to face.
shots.scene: Bo walks up to a supporting figure on an 1880s street, sticks out his hand in greeting, and says 'Hello!' in a speech bubble — no telephone anywhere in the frame — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: The telephone had given the world a new word.
shots.scene: Bo holds up a glowing 'HELLO' sign like a gift box, beaming at the viewer — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: And the word refused to stay on the wire.
shots.scene: Bo watches 'HELLO' break free from a copper wire and float off across a 1880s skyline — Bo stares after it — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: By the late 1880s, hello was appearing in books.
shots.scene: Bo pulls a leather-bound 1880s book off a library shelf, opens it, and points excitedly at the word 'hello' on the page — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: By the 1890s, it was in songs and plays.
shots.scene: Bo watches two supporting figures on a small stage — one in costume shouting 'Hello!' to applause from an audience — full-body wide shot, theater interior

shots.phrase: By 1900, children used it without ever owning a telephone.
shots.scene: Bo watches two young supporting figures in Edwardian dress greet each other with 'Hello!' speech bubbles in a park — no telephone anywhere near them — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: The word had completely outrun its own origin story.
shots.scene: Bo runs but the glowing 'HELLO' sign races far ahead of him, disappearing into the distance — Bo pants with hands on knees — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: No other word had ever traveled quite this way.
shots.scene: Bo stands before a large world map, tracing a glowing line from America outward in all directions — expression quietly awed — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Not through generations, not through religion, not through conquest.
shots.scene: Bo crosses out icons one by one on a chalkboard — a family tree, a church, a sword — shaking his head deliberately at each — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: It spread through copper wire in under twenty years.
shots.scene: Bo traces a glowing copper wire across a globe with one finger, watching 'HELLO' hop from city to city — expression amazed — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Today, Germany says hallo. France says allô.
shots.scene: Bo stands before a split world map — speech bubbles appear over Germany reading 'Hallo!' and over France reading 'Allô!' — Bo points at each one — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Latin America says aló. Almost every language borrowed it.
shots.scene: Bo gestures at a world map covered in 'hello' variations in different scripts and languages — his arms spread wide — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: And almost all of them got it through the telephone.
shots.scene: Bo traces a single copper wire backward from all the speech bubbles on the map, all converging back to one original wooden telephone — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: In every language, in every country, in every home.
shots.scene: Bo spreads both arms wide at the world map now filled with 'hello' in dozens of scripts — expression quietly triumphant — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Because of one man, with one phone, with one letter.
shots.scene: Bo holds up one finger, then a miniature telephone, then a folded letter — counting each item off carefully, expression building — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: One letter written in 1877 became the planet's greeting.
shots.scene: Bo holds a glowing letter envelope labeled '1877' while a glowing Earth rotates slowly in the background — Bo looks at it with quiet reverence — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: You say it every single day.
shots.scene: Bo waves hello to passersby at a sidewalk café table, same pose and framing as shot 1, same morning light — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: To strangers, to friends, to empty rooms.
shots.scene: Bo turns to wave at a stranger, a friend, then an empty chair — same framing as shot 2, same playful expression — full-body wide shot

shots.phrase: Hello. That is Edison's word. It is still winning.
shots.scene: Bo turns directly to the viewer, holds up a small card reading 'Edison 1877', points at the viewer with a knowing smile — same framing as shot 4 — full-body wide shot

character.name: Bo
character.appearance: mid-20s to early-30s man, short dark tousled hair, light stubble, round glasses, warm expressive face, average build
character.outfit: mustard-yellow t-shirt, dark blue jeans, white sneakers, brown cross-body satchel
character.role: explainer and viewer stand-in — appears in every shot, reacts to the story, addresses the viewer directly

style.clothing: Bo is fully locked across all 70 shots — mustard-yellow t-shirt, dark blue jeans, white sneakers, round glasses, brown cross-body satchel — no era adjustment ever. Supporting figures wear era-accurate late-19th-century clothing: Victorian frock coats, top hats, waistcoats, period shirtwaists, Edwardian children's dress. The contrast between Bo's modern clothes and the historical world around him is intentional and must be preserved in every frame.
style.background: Late-19th-century settings throughout the main story arc — cobblestone streets, gas-lit telephone exchanges, muddy river docks, Victorian parlors, music hall theaters, public libraries. Transitions to a world map setting for the global spread section. Warm sepia-to-golden palette for historical scenes. Modern clean tones return for opening and closing shots.
style.sky: Soft blue morning sky for opening and closing shots. Warm amber overcast for indoor Victorian historical scenes. Deep indigo star-flecked sky for the global spread and world map sequences.

voice.style: deep male narrator, calm, unhurried, engaged — slightly warmer than a documentary, like a friend who just found something remarkable out
